courses.title: Chemical Pathology
courses.description: Clinical interpretation of biochemical tests: water and electrolytes, acid–base, renal and liver disease, endocrine function, lipids, and tumour markers.

topics.title: Water, Sodium and Potassium Disorders
topics.summary: Hyponatraemia and hypernatraemia, SIADH, and hypo- and hyperkalaemia with management.

material.heading: Sodium
material.body: Hyponatraemia (Na+ < 135 mmol/L) is classified by volume status: hypovolaemic (vomiting, diarrhoea, diuretics — especially thiazides, Addison's disease, salt-losing nephropathy), euvolaemic (SIADH — causes include pneumonia, TB, meningitis, head injury, small-cell lung cancer, drugs such as carbamazepine and SSRIs; hypothyroidism; glucocorticoid deficiency) and hypervolaemic (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome). SIADH: low plasma osmolality with inappropriately concentrated urine (urine osmolality > 100 mOsm/kg) and high urine sodium (> 30 mmol/L) in a euvolaemic patient; treat with fluid restriction. Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizures, coma) needs hypertonic (3%) saline; correct chronic hyponatraemia slowly (no more than about 8–10 mmol/L in 24 hours) to avoid osmotic demyelination. Hypernatraemia (Na+ > 145) usually reflects water deficit — dehydration, diabetes insipidus — corrected slowly.

material.heading: Potassium
material.body: Hyperkalaemia (K+ > 5.5 mmol/L): causes include renal failure, potassium-sparing diuretics, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, Addison's disease, acidosis, tissue breakdown (rhabdomyolysis, tumour lysis, haemolysis), and spurious results from haemolysed samples or delayed separation. ECG: peaked T waves, flattened P waves, widened QRS, sine-wave pattern, cardiac arrest. Emergency treatment: IV calcium gluconate (stabilises myocardium), insulin with dextrose and nebulised salbutamol (shift K+ into cells), then removal (potassium binders, dialysis). Hypokalaemia (K+ < 3.5): diuretics, vomiting, diarrhoea, insulin therapy, hyperaldosteronism; features include weakness, ileus and arrhythmias (U waves); replace orally or with slow IV infusion.

topics.title: Acid–Base Disorders and Blood Gases
topics.summary: Interpreting arterial blood gases, anion gap, compensation and mixed disorders.

material.heading: Stepwise interpretation
material.body: Normal ABG: pH 7.35–7.45, PaCO2 4.7–6.0 kPa (35–45 mmHg), HCO3− 22–26 mmol/L, PaO2 > 10.6 kPa on air, base excess −2 to +2. Steps: (1) assess oxygenation; (2) acidaemia or alkalaemia from pH; (3) respiratory component (PaCO2) or metabolic (HCO3−/base excess) as the primary cause; (4) assess compensation — respiratory compensation for metabolic disorders is rapid (Winter's formula for metabolic acidosis: expected PaCO2 = 1.5 × HCO3− + 8 ± 2 mmHg); renal compensation for respiratory disorders takes days; (5) calculate the anion gap in metabolic acidosis.

material.heading: Causes
material.body: Raised anion gap metabolic acidosis (MUDPILES: methanol, uraemia, diabetic ketoacidosis, paraldehyde/propylene glycol, isoniazid/iron, lactic acidosis — shock, sepsis, severe malaria — ethylene glycol, salicylates). Normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic) acidosis: diarrhoea, renal tubular acidosis, ureterosigmoidostomy, excessive normal saline. Metabolic alkalosis: vomiting (loss of HCl — hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic), diuretics, hyperaldosteronism. Respiratory acidosis: hypoventilation — COPD, opioids, neuromuscular disease, chest wall disorders. Respiratory alkalosis: hyperventilation — anxiety, pain, early salicylate poisoning, pulmonary embolism, high altitude, pregnancy. Salicylate poisoning classically causes a mixed respiratory alkalosis and raised-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.
keyPoints: Salicylates: mixed respiratory alkalosis + metabolic acidosis

topics.title: Kidney Disease: Biochemical Assessment
topics.summary: Acute kidney injury, chronic kidney disease staging, proteinuria and renal stones.

material.heading: AKI and CKD
material.body: Acute kidney injury (KDIGO): rise in creatinine ≥ 26.5 µmol/L within 48 hours, or ≥ 1.5 × baseline within 7 days, or urine output < 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours. Causes are pre-renal (hypovolaemia — diarrhoea, haemorrhage, sepsis; urine sodium low, high urea:creatinine), intrinsic renal (acute tubular necrosis, glomerulonephritis, nephrotoxins — aminoglycosides, NSAIDs, contrast, herbal remedies; severe malaria and snakebite) and post-renal (obstruction — prostate enlargement, stones). Chronic kidney disease is abnormal kidney structure or function for > 3 months, staged by eGFR (G1 ≥ 90; G2 60–89; G3a 45–59; G3b 30–44; G4 15–29; G5 < 15 mL/min/1.73 m² — kidney failure) and albuminuria (A1–A3). Leading causes in Nigeria: hypertension, chronic glomerulonephritis, diabetes, HIV-associated nephropathy and sickle cell nephropathy. Complications: anaemia (low EPO), renal bone disease (high phosphate, low calcium, secondary hyperparathyroidism), hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis and fluid overload.
keyPoints: CKD causes: hypertension, GN, diabetes, HIVAN

material.heading: Proteinuria and stones
material.body: Proteinuria is quantified by urine protein:creatinine ratio (PCR) or albumin:creatinine ratio (ACR); nephrotic-range proteinuria is > 3.5 g/day (PCR > 300 mg/mmol), with hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and hyperlipidaemia. Glomerular haematuria with red cell casts indicates nephritis. Kidney stones: calcium oxalate (commonest, radio-opaque), calcium phosphate, uric acid (radiolucent; gout, tumour lysis), struvite/magnesium ammonium phosphate (urease-producing Proteus infection — staghorn calculi) and cystine (inherited cystinuria — hexagonal crystals). Investigations include serum calcium, urate, urine 24-hour calcium, oxalate, citrate and stone analysis.

topics.title: Endocrine Function Tests
topics.summary: Thyroid function tests, adrenal testing, calcium disorders and pituitary assessment.

material.heading: Thyroid and adrenal
material.body: TSH is the best first-line thyroid test. Primary hypothyroidism: high TSH, low free T4 (Hashimoto's thyroiditis, iodine deficiency, post-thyroidectomy/radioiodine). Subclinical hypothyroidism: high TSH, normal free T4. Primary hyperthyroidism: suppressed TSH, high free T4 and/or T3 (Graves' disease — TSH-receptor antibodies; toxic multinodular goitre). Secondary (pituitary) disease: low TSH with low free T4. Sick euthyroid syndrome occurs in severe illness. Adrenal: Cushing's syndrome is screened with the overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test, 24-hour urinary free cortisol or late-night salivary cortisol; Addison's disease is confirmed by a low cortisol that fails to rise after synacthen (ACTH stimulation test), with high ACTH. Primary aldosteronism: raised aldosterone:renin ratio.
keyPoints: TSH first; high TSH + low fT4 = primary hypothyroidism

material.heading: Calcium and pituitary
material.body: Correct total calcium for albumin (adjusted Ca = measured Ca + 0.02 × (40 − albumin g/L)). Hypercalcaemia: primary hyperparathyroidism (high calcium with high or inappropriately normal PTH; commonest in outpatients) and malignancy (low PTH, PTHrP or bone metastases; commonest in inpatients); also vitamin D excess, sarcoidosis and thiazides. Symptoms: 'bones, stones, abdominal groans and psychic moans'; treat severe cases with IV saline then bisphosphonates. Hypocalcaemia: hypoparathyroidism (post-thyroidectomy), vitamin D deficiency, CKD, acute pancreatitis; tetany, Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs, prolonged QT; treat with IV calcium gluconate. Pituitary: prolactinoma (raised prolactin), acromegaly (raised IGF-1; GH not suppressed by oral glucose), and hypopituitarism (dynamic testing).
keyPoints: Acromegaly: ↑IGF-1, GH not suppressed by glucose

topics.title: Lipids, Cardiac Markers and Tumour Markers
topics.summary: Lipid profile and cardiovascular risk, markers of myocardial injury and heart failure, and tumour markers.

material.heading: Lipids
material.body: A lipid profile includes total cholesterol, triglycerides, HDL cholesterol and LDL cholesterol (often calculated by the Friedewald equation: LDL = total cholesterol − HDL − TG/2.2 in mmol/L, invalid if TG > 4.5 mmol/L). Traditionally a fasting sample was used, especially for triglycerides. Raised LDL and low HDL increase cardiovascular risk; very high triglycerides (> 10 mmol/L) risk acute pancreatitis. Secondary causes of dyslipidaemia: diabetes, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestasis, alcohol and drugs (thiazides, steroids, some antiretrovirals). Treatment: lifestyle and statins (first-line for LDL lowering).

material.heading: Cardiac and tumour markers
material.body: Cardiac troponin (I or T) is the marker of choice for myocardial infarction: it rises within 3–6 hours, peaks at 12–24 hours and remains raised for 7–14 days; high-sensitivity assays allow rapid rule-out protocols, and a rise and/or fall is required. Troponin is also raised in myocarditis, pulmonary embolism, sepsis and renal failure. BNP/NT-proBNP helps diagnose heart failure. Tumour markers are mainly used for monitoring treatment and detecting recurrence rather than screening: AFP (hepatocellular carcinoma — common in Nigeria with hepatitis B; germ-cell tumours), β-hCG (choriocarcinoma, testicular tumours, molar pregnancy), PSA (prostate cancer — also raised in benign prostatic hyperplasia and prostatitis), CA-125 (ovarian cancer), CEA (colorectal cancer), CA 19-9 (pancreatic cancer), and paraproteins (myeloma).
keyPoints: Tumour markers: monitoring more than screening
PSA: prostate; CA-125: ovary; CEA: colon
